content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for cervical cancer prevention in the general population of women. However, HPV mRNA testing may also be utilized as an alternative. When implementing HPV mRNA testing, WHO suggests the following: it can be provided with or without triage, it should use samples collected by healthcare providers, and it should be conducted at five-year intervals. This recommendation is conditional and based on evidence with low certainty. HPV DNA testing remains the preferred screening method. Opting for HPV mRNA testing requires the capacity to ensure follow-up screenings every five years. Notably, no recommendation has been made for the use of HPV mRNA testing in women living with HIV due to insufficient evidence regarding its outcomes in this population. Cervical cancer is a significant cause of mortality among women worldwide. In 2020, approximately 604,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer, and 342,000 died from the disease. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 23 countries and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in 36 countries, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South America, and Southeast Asia. In May 2018, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for action to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem. This led to the development of the WHO Global Strategy, which was endorsed in August 2020. The strategy aims to achieve the following targets by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90% of women with cervical disease receiving appropriate treatment (90% of women with pre-cancer treated and 90% of women with invasive cancer managed). Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is characterized by cellular changes in the transformation zone of the cervix, typically caused by high-risk HPV infections, particularly strains 16 and 18, which account for over 70% of cervical cancers. CIN1 lesions, also known as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, are morphological correlates of HPV infections. Traditionally, cervical cancer screening has relied on cytology (Pap smear). Positive cytology results are confirmed through colposcopy, and treatment decisions are guided by biopsy and histological diagnosis. However, HPV DNA and mRNA testing are nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) that detect the presence of the virus. HPV DNA tests identify viral DNA, while HPV mRNA tests detect transcripts of the E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which are responsible for oncogenic transformation in epithelial cells. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types is essential for cervical oncogenesis. The carcinogenic process begins with the integration of viral DNA into the host cellular DNA, leading to the expression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins. These proteins degrade tumor suppressor proteins (pRb and p53), disrupt cell cycle regulation, and promote cellular immortalization, initiating carcinogenesis. The expression of E6 and E7 increases with the severity of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. HPV mRNA tests, such as the Aptima™ mRNA assay, detect pooled E6/E7 mRNA from high-risk HPV types and may offer greater specificity than HPV DNA tests. The Aptima™ assay can detect mRNA from 14 high-risk HPV types and process up to 250 tests in approximately five hours. A positive result indicates E6/E7 mRNA above the detection threshold, while a negative result indicates levels below the threshold with a positive internal control. The WHO Global Strategy emphasizes the importance of evidence-based strategies for cervical cancer prevention, including HPV testing and treatment interventions. The updated guidelines aim to improve national strategies for screening and treatment, particularly for women living with HIV and the general population. The guidelines also distinguish between the screen-and-treat approach, where treatment is based on a positive primary screening test, and the screen, triage, and treat approach, which involves a secondary triage test to confirm the need for treatment. The updated recommendations integrate HPV mRNA-based screening strategies and follow-up testing at 12 months post-treatment. These guidelines are intended for policymakers, healthcare professionals, and program managers to ensure the implementation of effective cervical cancer prevention strategies.
